name: British Heart Foundation: research and policy (charityevals, 2025-26)
summary: The British Heart Foundation is the UK's largest charitable funder of heart and circulatory research; this model covers its research grants (£96.2m in the year to March 2026) and its policy work, chiefly its long campaign for the UK's smokefree-generation law. Research is valued as a share of the global cardiovascular burden that a year of the field's research averts sooner, credited by BHF's share of the world's cardiovascular research funding (about 1%); policy as its share of the health gain of the Tobacco and Vapes Act. The result, about 0.06 years of healthy life per $1,000, is far below the site's global-health median because research results arrive after about 17 years, are shared with the whole field, and are counted as a past average at the next dollar's share; it sits near SoGive's figure for UK breast cancer research. It is dominated by judgment (how much of the burden a year of research averts, how many years sooner, BHF's share of the field), so the range is wide; its information, support and CPR work is the separate health-and-support model.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: BHF's research spending and its share of policy work in the year to 31 March 2026, with the cost of raising the money (fundraising and the shops' net loss) spread over all its charitable spending. From the audited accounts.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: The burden the research addresses: the world's cardiovascular disease, since a drug, device or guideline found in the UK is used worldwide.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: Research: the share of that burden a year of the field's research averts once adopted, how many years sooner it comes, after the wait from funding to practice. Policy: the smokefree-generation law, the health its cohorts gain and the share of the campaign that fell in this year.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Each branch has its own trust in the evidence and its own share of credit (Convention 4): BHF's share of the world's cardiovascular research funding for research, its share of everyone's resources behind the law for policy. The canonical rows are their outcome-weighted averages.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: Years of healthy life averted by the year's research and policy work, per dollar.

sections.title: Programmes with no outcome data
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for a programme that publishes no outcome data at all: it is valued at the result per dollar of the same kind of work elsewhere on the site, read live, and counts less by the shared slider "How much we count a programme we could only estimate from similar ones" (docs/normalization.md 2.12). A programme with some outcome data is modelled from it in the chain above, with wide ranges, never here.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only. The research result is a past average (what a year's grants buy, by what past research achieved), so the next dollar is valued at the shared share of it.

rows.label: Research expenditure, year to 31 March 2026 (£)

source.title: British Heart Foundation, Annual Report and Accounts 2025-26, group statement of financial activities

rows.explainer: Net research awards (£91.9m: £103.3m of new grants less the expected underspend and discounting of long grants) plus BHF's own research staff and support costs (£4.3m), as the accounts report them for the year (note 4, p. 125). The year's grants fund 247 awards across fellowships, programme, project and clinical grants and BHF's research centres (p. 67).

rows.label: Health expenditure (information, support, CPR, policy), year to 31 March 2026 (£)

source.title: British Heart Foundation, Annual Report and Accounts 2025-26, group statement of financial activities

rows.explainer: BHF's second charitable activity: awareness, the Heart Matters magazine, the nurse-led Heart Helpline, health information, CPR (RevivR) and the defibrillator network (The Circuit), healthcare implementation grants, and policy and influencing in the four UK nations (p. 67, p. 28-36). Only its policy share is in this model; the rest is british-heart-foundation-charityevals-health.

rows.label: Share of health expenditure that is policy and influencing work
rows.explainer: The accounts don't split health spending by activity. Policy and public affairs teams in four nations (England, Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland), campaigns and BHF's grants to Action on Smoking and Health are a small part of a £54m budget dominated by information, the magazine, the helpline, CPR and implementation grants (£7.8m of health awards, note 11). Our judgment, anchored on a team of a few dozen people at UK charity pay (staff and support costs in health are £12.5m in all, note 4), with grants to ASH on top. The same judgment is in british-heart-foundation-charityevals-health and sets the programme weights in charities/british-heart-foundation.json: change all three together.

rows.label: Spending on research and policy, year to 31 March 2026 (US$)
rows.explainer: Research plus the policy share of health spending, in dollars at the 2025 yearly average rate (the year runs April 2025 to March 2026).

rows.label: Total charitable expenditure, year to 31 March 2026 (£)

source.title: British Heart Foundation, Annual Report and Accounts 2025-26, group statement of financial activities

rows.explainer: Research and health together: everything BHF spends on its charitable purposes.

rows.label: Net loss of the shops, year to 31 March 2026 (£)

source.title: British Heart Foundation, Annual Report and Accounts 2025-26, statement of financial activities summary
source.quote: Retail net (loss)/profit comprises retail net loss of £(6.7)m (2025: £0.0m) and income from donations received in BHF shops of £3.4m (2025: £3.6m)

rows.explainer: BHF runs the UK's largest charity retailer (651 shops). The shops count by their net contribution, not their gross trading (£240.1m of retail costs against similar sales): this year they lost £6.7m on trading (sales less costs), a cost the charity's other income covered, so it is spread over the charitable work like fundraising. Cash donated in the shops (£3.4m) is a donation, not trading, so it isn't netted against the loss. BHF announced in June 2026 the proposed closure of about 150 shops.

rows.explainer: Everything the year's charitable work cost once raising the money is included, with the shops at their net result rather than their gross turnover and costs.

Overhead multiplier (total ÷ program expenses)
rows.explainer: Spreads fundraising and the shops' loss over the charitable work in proportion to its cost (support costs are already allocated to research and health in the accounts).

rows.label: Cost of research and policy, including overhead
World burden of cardiovascular disease, DALYs per year (2021)

source.title: TCTMD, CVD claimed 20 million lives in 2021, but disease burden varies globally (reporting Lindstrom et al., JACC 2022, GBD 2021)
source.quote: responsible for more than 20 million deaths and more than 400 million disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) lost in 2021

rows.explainer: Heart and circulatory disease worldwide (ischaemic heart disease, stroke, heart failure and the rest), GBD 2021: more than 400 million DALYs a year. The whole world, because BHF's results (drugs, devices, guidelines) are used wherever such advances reach; uptake outside rich countries is lower, and that is in share_burden_addressable, not here. The JACC paper itself is paywalled, so we use the reported figure with a range above it.

rows.label: Share of the burden the advances from one year of the field's research avert each year once in use
rows.explainer: One judgment, the product of how much of the burden the kind of advances funded address and the chance a year's portfolio delivers one (split below for reading). Anchors: age-standardised cardiovascular death rates in rich countries have fallen about 2% a year for decades, and the IMPACT models attribute roughly half of the UK's fall in coronary deaths to treatments (statins, blood-pressure drugs, stents, thrombolysis), the rest to risk factors research also shaped; worldwide, where most of the burden is and uptake is low, research-driven gains are a fraction of that. So a year of the world's research adds of the order of a few tenths of a percent of the global burden averted: 0.3%, 0.05% to 1%.

rows.label: Share of that burden the advances from a year of the field's research avert once adopted
rows.explainer: For reading: the share of the burden the kind of advances funded (a new drug class, a device, a care pathway) address at the uptake they reach, a few percent each (SGLT2 inhibitors or PCSK9 inhibitors in their indications, primary angioplasty). The result reads only its product with p_success (share_burden_averted_per_research_year), so this split doesn't add a second range.

rows.label: Implied probability a year's portfolio of the field turns into such an advance in practice (for reading)
rows.explainer: The judged product over the judged share addressed: about 6%. For comparison, about 1 in 4 cardiovascular drugs entering phase 3 and well under 1 in 10 from phase 1 reach approval (Wong, Siah and Lo, Biostatistics 2019); BHF's portfolio is mostly basic and translational science.

rows.label: Years sooner the advance arrives because the field is funded this year
rows.explainer: Without a year of funding, the same advances would come later from the following years' research, industry and other countries; this is how much later. Its credit is split by BHF's share of the field's funding (research_attribution_share_shared), and it already answers "would it have happened anyway" (Convention 5), so there is no counterfactual adjustment as well. Anchored on the returns-to-research reference class: with the rest of the chain, 5 years makes a pound of BHF research about as productive in health as the 9% health-gain return of UK cardiovascular research implies in UK gains alone (ref_dalys_per_gbp against research_dalys_per_gbp_credited); 2 to 15 years.

rows.label: Years from the funding until the result is in practice

source.title: News-Medical, New report shows the financial and social value of investing in medical research (on HERG, OHE and RAND Europe, Medical Research: What's it worth?, 2008)
source.quote: a time lag between research expenditure and eventual health benefits of approximately 17 years.

rows.explainer: The lag the UK study of cardiovascular research found between research spending and health benefit; UK cancer research had about 15 years (Glover et al. 2014: an elapsed time of 15 years), and screening and guideline work is quicker (Morris, Wooding and Grant 2011). Discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the result is in practice
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Discounted years brought forward
Expected DALYs averted by the year's research of the whole field (before adjustments)
Reference class: health-gain return on UK cardiovascular research (internal rate of return)

source.title: Glover et al. (2014), BMC Medicine 12:99 (Europe PMC full text)
source.quote: This produced a best-estimate IRR of 10%, compared with 9% previously estimated for cardiovascular disease research.

rows.explainer: For reading only (the sanity bound of references/families/medical-research.md): UK cardiovascular research's return in UK health gains, 9% a year; cancer's 10% is the high end.

rows.label: Reference class: lag from research spending to health gain
rows.explainer: The same 17-year lag as the chain.

rows.label: Reference class: the study's value of a QALY (£)

source.title: News-Medical, New report shows the financial and social value of investing in medical research (on Medical Research: What's it worth?, 2008)
source.quote: Quality Adjusted Life Years (QALY), estimated by NICE to be worth around £25,000 each.

rows.explainer: The study's own conversion from health to money, used only to turn its return back into QALYs for the check; it moves nothing on the result's path.

rows.label: Reference class: UK healthy years per £ of research the return implies (for reading)
rows.explainer: A 9% return with a 17-year lag means each £ buys a stream of about £0.39 of UK health a year from year 17 on; at £25,000 a QALY and the shared discount rate that is about 0.0002 healthy years per £, in the UK alone, with UK research credited with 17% of UK gains (Glover et al.: "We related 17% of the annual NMB estimated to be attributable to UK research").

rows.label: The chain's healthy years per £ of BHF research, after its adjustments (for reading)
rows.explainer: Against ref_dalys_per_gbp: the chain gives about the same. The two count different things: the reference credits UK research with 17% of UK gains, far above the UK's few percent of the world's cardiovascular research funding, while the chain credits BHF its funding share of world gains. We take the agreement as the check and add no world spillover on top, since the 17% credit already counts UK research generously and uptake outside rich countries is low. In numbers: for the chain to match a UK-only reference while crediting BHF only its ~1% of world funding, world gains must be about ten times UK gains, plausible given the UK's small share of the world's cardiovascular burden and much lower uptake elsewhere. HERG's 9% is net of NHS treatment costs, so the reference is a lower bound on gross health gains.

rows.label: Advocacy: people aged 14 to 30 in England (2021)

source.title: DHSC, Tobacco and Vapes Bill impact assessment (March 2024; superseded by the November 2024 assessment of the reintroduced bill)
source.quote: The population of those aged 14 to 30 is 11,777,381

rows.explainer: The age group the impact assessment models the law's effect on smoking uptake in, from ONS 2021 mid-year estimates; with the number of single years of age it gives one year's cohort.

rows.label: Advocacy: single years of age from 14 to 30

source.title: DHSC, Tobacco and Vapes Bill impact assessment (March 2024; superseded by the November 2024 assessment of the reintroduced bill)
source.quote: The population of those aged 14 to 30 is 11,777,381

rows.explainer: Ages 14 to 30 inclusive are 17 single years, so the band divided by 17 is an average cohort.

rows.label: Advocacy: UK population ÷ England's

source.title: DHSC, Tobacco and Vapes Bill impact assessment (March 2024; superseded by the November 2024 assessment of the reintroduced bill)
source.quote: all the England estimates have been uplifted by 1.19 to provide estimates for the costs and benefits of the smokefree generation policy to the UK.

rows.explainer: The Act covers the whole UK; the impact assessment scales England by population, and so do we.

rows.label: Advocacy: people per year brought under the smokefree-generation law (one UK birth cohort)
rows.explainer: The Tobacco and Vapes Act (Royal Assent April 2026) bans the sale of tobacco to anyone born on or after 1 January 2009. Each year the law is brought forward covers one more birth cohort, about 820,000 people in the UK; so the yearly flow the win counts is one cohort, and $win_years_counted counts the years.

rows.label: Advocacy: share of a covered cohort kept from smoking
rows.explainer: The impact assessment's central scenario (a 30% fall in the yearly rate of taking up smoking below the age of sale, picked with 14 tobacco-control experts and chosen over stronger scenarios to allow for underage sales and proxy purchases, paras 154-161) takes smoking among 14 to 30 year olds from 9.2% in the baseline to effectively zero, "9.2 percentage points lower in 2056" (para. 169). That is the high end. Our best guess, 8 points, takes a little off for a baseline already falling faster than the assessment's flat steady state (a criticism made to the Public Bill Committee); leakage is not taken off again here or in adv_evidence_adj. The low end, 2.5 points, is the assessment's weakest scenario (Scenario 5, 6.7% against 9.2%, Table 27). The figures are from the March 2024 impact assessment; the November 2024 one for the reintroduced bill keeps the same smokefree-generation modelling.

rows.label: Advocacy: lifetime DALYs lost per person who smokes as a young adult
rows.explainer: Doll et al.'s 50-year follow-up of British doctors (BMJ 2004): lifelong smokers die about 10 years sooner, and stopping at 30 avoids almost all of that, at 40 most of it. Many young smokers stop, so a person smoking at 14 to 30 loses a few healthy years on average, deaths and illness from heart disease, cancer and lung disease together. Check against the impact assessment: with the rest of the branch a covered UK cohort gains about 170,000 DALYs undiscounted (824,000 × 7% × 3), about 95,000 at the government's 1.5% over 40 years; the assessment's own figure, deaths only and only those before 2100, is about 950,000 QALYs in present value (£66.7bn at £70,000) over all the cohorts it covers, most of whose smoking deaths fall after 2100, so roughly ten cohorts' worth by our figure. Consistent within the range.

rows.label: Advocacy: years from the law biting on a cohort until its health gains
rows.explainer: Smoking kills and disables mostly in middle and old age: the impact assessment finds "no health benefits would be expected until 2044" (para. 178), 17 years after the law starts, with gains rising to 2100. A cohort kept from smoking at 18 has its gains mostly at 50 to 80, about 40 years later. Discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Advocacy: DALYs averted per person in a covered cohort (lifetime, discounted to the law's start)
rows.explainer: The share kept from smoking times the healthy years a young smoker loses, discounted over the decades until those years come. Per cohort member, so multiplied by one cohort per year counted.

rows.label: Advocacy: share of all the campaigning behind the law done in this year
rows.explainer: The law is won (Royal Assent April 2026, three weeks after the year ends), so the question is how much of the win this year's work bought. The bill was introduced in November 2024 and spent this year in the House of Lords, the last stretch of a campaign that ran from the 2023 plan (and of decades of tobacco-control work before it); BHF's share of the people and money behind it is in adv_attribution_share_shared. A fifth, from about four years of active campaigning with the final year weighing more.

rows.label: Advocacy: years a won reform counts
rows.explainer: The site's one answer (docs/normalization.md 2.9).

rows.label: Advocacy: years from the year modelled until the law takes effect
rows.explainer: The sale ban starts on 1 January 2027 (the impact assessment's appraisal starts on that date), about a year after the middle of the year modelled. The longer wait until the health gains is in adv_dalys_per_person_year.

rows.label: Advocacy: discounted years of impact
Expected DALYs averted by advocacy (before adjustments)
Research: evidence adjustment, a multiplier
rows.explainer: The research chain rests on judgments calibrated to returns-to-research studies, which their authors call best-case estimates (they credit research with health gains that also came from changes in behaviour and care, and take the best-documented diseases). 0.7, as the template's default for a chain anchored on aggregate studies rather than this charity's own results; the range runs to face value.

rows.label: Research: BHF's share of the world's cardiovascular research funding
rows.explainer: The years brought forward are the whole field's, so BHF is credited with its share of all funders' spending on it (about $127m of research a year). Anchors: BHF funded 52% (£85m) of UK public and charity cardiovascular research in 2022 (UKCRC, via BHF); the US NIH spends about $2.9bn a year on cardiovascular research and EU public and charity funders at least €1bn (CardioScape, 2010-2012), with Japan, China, Canada and Australia on top: about $5-6bn of non-commercial research. Industry is counted in full: it pays about 58% of US biomedical research (Moses et al., JAMA 2015), so all funders together spend about $13bn a year on cardiovascular research, of which BHF is about 1%. The range runs from industry at twice that share (0.5%) to the non-commercial funders alone (2%).

rows.label: Advocacy: evidence adjustment, a multiplier
rows.explainer: The effect of a generational sale ban is modelled, not observed (New Zealand repealed its own before it took effect); underage sales and leakage are already in the assessment's central scenario and adv_prevalence_cut, so this covers the rest: substitution by vaping (which the same Act regulates) and the chance of later repeal. 0.7, as the research branch.

rows.label: Advocacy: BHF's share of everyone's resources behind the law
rows.explainer: The government proposed and drafted the law, Parliament passed it, and many groups campaigned (Action on Smoking and Health, Cancer Research UK, the royal colleges, directors of public health, BHF). BHF part-funds ASH and campaigned itself; it says the law "would not have materialised without constant pressure from ASH, ourselves and other partners" (annual report p. 35). Government staff time counts among the resources (Convention 2). One in twenty, from BHF being one of the two largest health charities in a coalition of dozens behind a government bill.

rows.label: Research: DALYs credited to BHF
Advocacy: DALYs credited to BHF
This charity's share of the resources behind the outcome (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.explainer: BHF's share of the field's funding for research and of the campaign's resources for policy, weighted by each branch's DALYs; each branch applies its own.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.explainer: Each branch's own trust in its evidence, weighted by the DALYs it credits.

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1 in both branches: for research, the years brought forward already say how much later the advance would have come without the year's funding; for the law, $win_years_counted says how much later it would have come (Convention 5: one question, counted once).

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the averages above: exactly the credited DALYs over the DALYs before adjustment.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Benefits not counted: the Act's limits on youth vaping, second-hand smoke averted (both left out by the impact assessment's health figures), the research workforce and infrastructure BHF trains and builds that later research uses. Harms: research effort drawn from other diseases (BHF's leverage of other funders' money is not counted as a gain either). Small and positive on balance.

rows.label: Value in units of value (none: the burden is counted in DALYs), in GiveWell units of value (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: 0: both branches count deaths and illness together in DALYs (GBD burden; DALYs per smoker), and the model counts no income gains.

rows.label: Value in units of value (none: the burden is counted in DALYs), in healthy years
rows.explainer: The bridge from UoV into healthy years (docs/normalization.md 2.6): fixed, don't edit.

rows.label: Life satisfaction (none measured), in wellbeing-adjusted life years (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: 0: neither branch has evidence in life-satisfaction terms; their good is counted as healthy years.

rows.label: Life satisfaction (none measured), in healthy years
rows.explainer: The bridge from WELLBYs into healthy years (docs/normalization.md 2.6): fixed, don't edit.

rows.label: Healthy years counted directly (before adjustments)
Years of healthy life
rows.explainer: Each branch with its own adjustments (Convention 4), plus any bridged outcome at the average adjustment, times the unmodelled share.

rows.label: Years of healthy life per dollar
BHF's own staff pay as a share of research cost

source.title: British Heart Foundation, Annual Report and Accounts 2025-26, note 4 gross expenditure

rows.explainer: Research: £91.9m of awards, £1.9m of BHF staff costs, £0.7m other direct costs, £1.7m of allocated support costs (almost all staff), so BHF's own staff are about 4% of research cost; policy work is more staff-heavy, hence the high end. The researchers the grants pay are university staff, whose pay is the grants' cost, not BHF staff's forgone salary.

rows.label: Pay gap versus comparable jobs elsewhere
rows.explainer: BHF's staff are UK charity staff (grant managers, policy and support staff): the shared gap for UK charities.

rows.label: Salary forgone by staff (in-kind donation)
How much the next dollar does compared with the average dollar so far
rows.explainer: This model's cost per outcome is the charity's past spending over what it won (estimate_basis past_average), so the next dollar is valued at the shared share of the average (docs/normalization.md 2.10). 1 in `published`: what the past average itself says.

Years of healthy life per dollar you give
rows.explainer: The modelled programmes' result for their share of the spending, plus the programmes with no outcome data (the proxy section).

rows.label: Spending on programmes with no outcome data at all, in the year modelled

source.title: British Heart Foundation, Annual Report and Accounts 2025-26, group statement of financial activities

rows.explainer: 0: research and policy both have outcome data to build the chain on. BHF's information and support work, which has none, is proxied in the health-and-support model (british-heart-foundation-charityevals-health), not here.

rows.label: Result per dollar of comparable programmes on the site (units of value per dollar you give)
rows.explainer: Not used here (no proxied spending). The same peers as the health-and-support model's proxy: ranked best guesses only (SoGive's central estimate for Breast Cancer Now, Founders Pledge's for Action for Happiness).

rows.explainer: The modelled programmes' result counts for the rest of the spending.

rows.explainer: The bridge from units of value into this model's unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6); the unit's conversion cancels it, so these programmes count exactly their peers' value. Don't edit it.
